India.text: Its name comes, via Greek and Persian, from Sindhu, the Sanskrit word for "river".
India.evidence: Further etymons are: Hellenistic Greek India (Ἰνδία); Ancient Greek Indos (Ἰνδός), or the River Indus; Achaemenian Old Persian Hinduš (an eastern province of the Achaemenid Empire); and Sanskrit Sindhu, or "river," but specifically the Indus river, and by extension its well-settled basin.

China.text: A common theory traces the name China to Qin, whose imperial dynasty lasted only fifteen years.
China.evidence: In 1655, the missionary Martino Martini suggested that the word China is derived ultimately from the ancient state of Qin. This remains a common etymology. ... In 221, its ruler Qin Shi Huang proclaimed himself the first emperor (皇帝; Huángdì) and founded the Qin dynasty. ... The dynasty lasted only fifteen years, falling soon after his death from revolts and civil war.

United States.text: Under the Homestead Acts, nearly 10% of its land was given away free to about 1.6 million settlers.
United States.evidence: This was accelerated by the Homestead Acts, through which nearly 10 percent of the total land area of the United States was given away free to some 1.6 million homesteaders.

Indonesia.text: The 1815 eruption of its Mount Tambora was followed by global cooling and the Year Without a Summer.
Indonesia.evidence: The Toba super-eruption about 74,000 years ago is one of the largest known explosive eruptions in Earth's history, and the 1815 eruption of Mount Tambora was followed by global cooling and the Year Without a Summer in 1816.

Pakistan.text: The name was coined in a 1933 pamphlet as an acronym of Panjab, Afghania, Kashmir, Sindh and Baluchistan.
Pakistan.evidence: The name Pakistan was coined by Choudhry Rahmat Ali, a Pakistan Movement activist, who in January 1933 first published it (originally as "Pakstan") in a pamphlet Now or Never, using it as an acronym. Rahmat Ali explained: "It is composed of letters taken from the names of all our homelands, Indian and Asian, Panjab, Afghania, Kashmir, Sindh, and Baluchistan."

Nigeria.text: The name was coined in 1897 by journalist Flora Shaw; other proposals included "Niger Sudan" and "Central Sudan".
Nigeria.evidence: This name was coined on 8 January 1897, by the British journalist Flora Shaw. ... Before Flora Shaw suggested the name Nigeria, other proposed names included Royal Niger Company Territories, Central Sudan, Niger Empire, Niger Sudan, and Hausa Territories.

Brazil.text: Told by Europe to leave Rio, Portugal's exiled court made Brazil a kingdom in 1815 to justify staying.
Brazil.evidence: In 1809, in retaliation for being forced into exile, the Prince Regent ordered the conquest of French Guiana. ... With the end of the Peninsular War in 1814, the courts of Europe demanded that Queen Maria I and Prince Regent John return to Portugal, deeming it unfit for the head of an ancient European monarchy to reside in a colony. In 1815, to justify continuing to live in Brazil, where the royal court had thrived for six years, the Crown established the United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves, thus creating a pluricontinental transatlantic monarchic state.

Bangladesh.text: Its name was sung in patriotic songs decades before independence, including one by Rabindranath Tagore in 1905.
Bangladesh.evidence: The etymology of Bangladesh ("Bengali country") can be traced to the early 20th century, when Bengali patriotic songs, such as Aaji Bangladesher Hridoy by Rabindranath Tagore and Namo Namo Namo Bangladesh Momo by Kazi Nazrul Islam, used the term in 1905 and 1932 respectively. ... Bangladesh became a sovereign nation on 16 December 1971.

Russia.text: Its old name, Rus', is thought to come via the Finnish word for Sweden from Old Norse for "related to rowing".
Russia.evidence: The oldest endonyms used were Rus' (Русь) and Russkaya zemlya (Русская земля, 'Russian land'). ... The name is considered a borrowing from Finnic Ruotsi ('Sweden'), in turn derived from Old Norse rōþs- ('related to rowing').

Mexico.text: Maize, tomatoes and beans were all first domesticated here.
Mexico.evidence: Mexico is the site of the domestication of maize, tomato, and beans, which produced an agricultural surplus.
